title: The Karorsinghia misl
hookLine: a misl of the Doaba lands

lines: THE DOABA, BETWEEN THE BEAS AND THE SUTLEJ.
cards: Wedding drums in one village, and the next village over can hear them. Wheat, sugarcane, mango groves: flat green farmland between the Beas and the Sutlej. Punjabis call it the Doaba.
A family there knows the families around it, and whose grandfather dug which well. In the misl years, riders from those villages saddled up together and fought as one band.
Their neighbors knew them by their leader's name, and the land knew them as its own.

teach.h: NAMED FOR A LEADER: KARORA SINGH.
teach.b: Sikh histories say this misl was named for one of its leaders, Karora Singh. So the name carries a person, but the band belonged to a place. Its riders came largely from the Doaba, and that is where their strength sat.
A misl was not an army on a map. It was farmers' sons, cousins and neighbors, men who knew which well was sweet and whose field bordered whose.
They rode for a village they could name, and when danger passed, they went home to it. Then a later leader, Baghel Singh. Tradition says he took the band far beyond the Doaba, all the way to Delhi.
The story Sikhs tell about him there is not mainly about conquest. Tradition says he sought out the places in the city tied to the Gurus, and saw that they were marked.
Gurdwaras stand at such places in Delhi today, and Sikh memory links some of them to his search.
A band rooted in one patch of farmland reached a far city, and what it is remembered for there is remembering.
And the plainest point: home ground shaped a misl.

teach.h: HOME GROUND GIVES EACH BAND ITS ACCENT.
teach.b: A band of the Doaba carried its fields, wells and neighbors into its fights and its peace.
The faith was the same in every band. Place gave each one its own accent.

how: Sikh histories describe each misl by its leaders and its home country; families in Punjab sometimes still remember which misl their village rode with.

o: finding the places tied to the Gurus and seeing them marked.

practice: Bring to mind the place you come from, or where you live now: not the map of it, but the weather, the sound outside your window early in the morning, the road you take without thinking.
Notice one way it has shaped you, how you talk, what you eat, what you expect from strangers; you don't have to like it, just notice it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
